arithmetic.question: What is this kind of problem asking you to find?
options: How a quantity changes after an event
Which object in the story is largest
How many equal groups there are
arithmetic.why: Addition and subtraction problems describe a starting amount and a change, so you want the amount after that change.

arithmetic.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Add every number that appears in the text
Name the starting amount and what changes
Guess from the biggest answer option shown
arithmetic.why: Naming the start and the change tells you whether to add or subtract, instead of combining every number automatically.

arithmetic.question: Which check fits this kind of problem best?
options: Check that the answer is a round number
Check that the answer uses every number given
Check if the result should be bigger or smaller
arithmetic.why: If something is taken away the result must be smaller than the start, and if something is added it must be bigger.

division.question: What does a division problem usually ask you to find?
options: How much bigger one amount is than another
How many items there are in total
The size or the number of equal groups
division.why: Division splits a known total into equal groups, so the unknown is either the group size or how many groups fit.

division.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Find the total and what must be equal
Multiply the two largest numbers you can see
Subtract the smaller number from the larger one
division.why: You can only share fairly once you know the total and whether the number of groups or their size is fixed.

division.question: Which check fits a division answer best?
options: The answer is smaller than every given number
Your answer times the divisor gives the total
The answer appears somewhere in the problem text
division.why: Multiplication undoes division, so multiplying your answer back must rebuild the original total exactly.

geometry_measurement.question: What should you decide first about a shape question?
options: Whether the shape looks bigger than the others
Whether it asks about the boundary or inside
Whether the numbers given are odd or even
geometry_measurement.why: Perimeter measures the boundary and area measures the inside, so they need different calculations and different units.

geometry_measurement.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Multiply every length that appears together
Add the numbers and divide by two
Label the known lengths on a sketch
geometry_measurement.why: A labelled sketch shows which lengths you know and which single missing length to find next.

geometry_measurement.question: Which check fits a perimeter or area answer?
options: Area uses square units and length does not
The answer should be a whole number
The answer matches the longest side given
geometry_measurement.why: Area counts unit squares, so it is measured in square units, while perimeter is a length in ordinary units.

logical_constraints.question: What does a logic problem ask you to find?
options: Options that satisfy every condition together
The option that satisfies the first condition
The option with the largest number
logical_constraints.why: A valid answer must survive all the conditions at once, not just the one you read first.

logical_constraints.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Pick the option that sounds most likely
Combine all the conditions into one guess
Write each condition as a separate check
logical_constraints.why: Separate checks let you test a candidate against each rule without forgetting any of them.

logical_constraints.question: When can you cross out a candidate?
options: When it feels less likely than the others
When you can name the condition it breaks
When it uses a number from the problem
logical_constraints.why: A candidate is ruled out only by a specific broken condition; otherwise it may still be the answer.

multiplication.question: What does a multiplication problem usually describe?
options: One amount taken away from another
Several groups that all have the same size
Two amounts compared to find a difference
multiplication.why: Multiplication counts a total made of equal groups, so you need the number of groups and the size of each.

multiplication.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Write the number of groups and group size
Add together all the numbers you can see
Pick the largest number and double it
multiplication.why: Keeping the number of groups separate from the size of each group stops you from mixing them up.

multiplication.question: Which check fits a multiplication answer?
options: The answer must be an even number
The answer is smaller than each factor
Repeated addition of the groups gives this total
multiplication.why: Adding one group again and again, once per group, must give the same total as your multiplication.

order_of_operations.question: What does an expression with several operations ask for?
options: Each operation done strictly from left to right
The largest result you can possibly make
One value, following agreed priority rules
order_of_operations.why: Everyone follows one agreed order, brackets and multiplication before addition, so the expression has exactly one value.

order_of_operations.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Calculate the first two numbers you see
Look for brackets and multiplication first
Add all the numbers, then multiply
order_of_operations.why: Brackets and multiplication have priority, so finding them first tells you which part to calculate before the rest.

order_of_operations.question: Which check fits this kind of problem?
options: Every operation was used exactly once
The answer is bigger than every number
The answer is the same read backwards
order_of_operations.why: Rewriting the expression after each step shows whether an operation was skipped or used twice.

patterns.question: What does a pattern problem ask you to find?
options: A rule that explains every step shown
The largest number in the sequence shown
The step that looks the most different
patterns.why: A pattern is described by a rule, and the rule must work for every step, not only the last one.

patterns.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Copy the last step and change it slightly
Describe what stays the same and what changes
Add the first and last visible terms
patterns.why: Separating what stays fixed from what changes reveals the repeating block or the constant difference.

patterns.question: Which check fits your proposed rule?
options: It produces the very last step shown
It gives a number that looks reasonable
It works on several steps, not just one
patterns.why: A rule that fits only one step may be a coincidence, so test it on several earlier steps too.

proportional_reasoning.question: What does a proportion problem ask you to keep?
options: The same difference between the two amounts
The same total of both quantities
The same scale factor between two quantities
proportional_reasoning.why: Quantities in proportion grow by multiplying, so the ratio between them stays fixed while the difference changes.

proportional_reasoning.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Find the two quantities that change together
Add the same amount to both quantities
Guess the answer from the biggest option
proportional_reasoning.why: Spotting which two quantities are linked lets you compare one group with the requested number of groups.

proportional_reasoning.question: Which check fits a proportion answer?
options: Each quantity changed by the same amount
Each quantity changed by the same factor
The answer is larger than both quantities
proportional_reasoning.why: If one quantity triples, the linked quantity must also triple; otherwise the relationship has changed.

spatial_reasoning.question: What does a spatial problem usually ask you to track?
options: How many colours the picture contains
How shapes or parts move or change view
Which shape has the longest outline drawn
spatial_reasoning.why: Spatial problems are about following positions and orientations through a movement, fold or change of viewpoint.

spatial_reasoning.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Compare only the overall outline of shapes
Count all the sides you can see
Choose one distinctive corner or mark to follow
spatial_reasoning.why: Following one distinctive feature through the movement makes it easier to tell a rotation from a reflection.

spatial_reasoning.question: Which check fits your chosen answer?
options: Several features match, not only the outline
The outline looks roughly the same size
It is the most symmetric picture shown
spatial_reasoning.why: Reflections and rotations can share an outline, so checking several features avoids choosing a mirror image by mistake.

systematic_counting.question: What does a counting problem ask you to find?
options: How many different valid cases exist
The largest case that follows the rules
Which single case is the correct one
systematic_counting.why: Counting problems ask for the number of possibilities, so each valid case must be found exactly once.

systematic_counting.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Write down cases in whatever order they come
Multiply the numbers given in the problem
Keep one feature fixed while listing cases
systematic_counting.why: Fixing one feature at a time gives an organised list, which makes missing or repeated cases easy to spot.

systematic_counting.question: Which check fits your count?
options: Your total is close to the biggest option
Each case follows the rules and appears once
Each case uses different digits or objects
systematic_counting.why: A careful count includes every valid case, excludes invalid ones, and never counts the same case twice.

sample-1.question: What does the question ask you to find?
options: How many apples are in each bag
How many apples Anna has at the end
How many apples Anna ate in total
sample-1.why: The question asks how many are left, which is the amount after Anna eats some apples.

sample-1.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Find how many apples are in the bags
Add the numbers three, four and two
Take two away from the four apples
sample-1.why: You need the starting total of apples before you can take away the ones Anna eats.

sample-1.question: Which check fits your final answer?
options: It is bigger than the total in the bags
It equals the number of apples in one bag
It is less than the total in the bags
sample-1.why: Anna eats some apples, so she must end with fewer apples than were in the bags at the start.

sample-2.question: What does the question ask you to find?
options: The result of working left to right
The sum of all three numbers shown
The single value of the whole expression
sample-2.why: An expression has exactly one value, found by following the agreed order of operations.

sample-2.question: Which part should you calculate first?
options: The addition two plus three
The multiplication three times four
Whichever operation is written first
sample-2.why: Multiplication comes before addition, so the multiplication is calculated before anything is added.

sample-2.question: Which check fits your final answer?
options: Each operation was used exactly once
The answer is the largest one possible
The answer equals five times four
sample-2.why: Each operation in the expression must be used once, and in the right order, to give its value.

sample-3.question: What does the question ask you to find?
options: The space inside the square
The length around the square
The length of one diagonal
sample-3.why: Area measures the inside of a shape, while the perimeter you are given measures its boundary.

sample-3.question: Which first move is most useful?
options: Multiply the perimeter by itself
Divide the perimeter by two
Find the length of one side
sample-3.why: A square has four equal sides, so the perimeter tells you one side length, which you need for the area.

sample-3.question: Which check fits your final answer?
options: It is in centimetres, like the perimeter
It is in square centimetres
It is four times the perimeter
sample-3.why: Area counts unit squares, so the answer must be measured in square centimetres, not centimetres.

sample-4.question: Què et demana la pregunta?
options: Quants cromos dóna en Pau
Quants cromos li queden a en Pau
Quants cromos té la seva germana
sample-4.why: La pregunta vol saber quants cromos li queden després de donar-ne alguns a la germana.

sample-4.question: Quin primer pas és més útil?
options: Sumar tots els nombres que apareixen
Triar l'opció més gran de totes
Identificar quants en tenia i quants en dóna
sample-4.why: Saber la quantitat inicial i la que canvia et diu si has de sumar o restar.

sample-4.question: Quina comprovació encaixa amb la teva resposta?
options: Ha de ser menys de quinze cromos
Ha de ser més de quinze cromos
Ha de ser igual als cromos donats
sample-4.why: En Pau dóna cromos, així que n'ha de tenir menys que els quinze que tenia al principi.

sample-5.question: Què et demana la pregunta?
options: Quin és el nombre més gran possible
Quina és la suma de les xifres
Quants nombres compleixen la condició
sample-5.why: Has de comptar quants nombres de dues xifres tenen la suma demanada, no trobar-ne només un.

sample-5.question: Quin primer pas és més útil?
options: Fixar la xifra de les desenes i provar
Multiplicar els nombres que surten a l'enunciat
Escriure nombres a l'atzar fins a cansar-te
sample-5.why: Si fixes les desenes una per una, cada cas té una sola xifra de les unitats possible i no te'n deixes cap.

sample-5.question: Quina comprovació encaixa amb el teu recompte?
options: Has comptat també nombres que comencen per zero
Cada nombre compleix la regla i surt una vegada
El total coincideix amb l'opció més gran
sample-5.why: Un nombre de dues xifres no pot començar per zero, i cada nombre vàlid es compta exactament una vegada.
